heading: PROPHET YAḤYĀ (AS)
title: THE WISDOM OF A YOUNG HEART
themes: Scripture • Wisdom • Compassion • Purity • Duty to Parents • Humility • The Hereafter
scope: 8 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 9 SELECTED QUR’ANIC VERSES
introduction: Volume Twenty-Three follows our learning journey from Prophet Zakariyyā (AS) to his son, Prophet Yaḥyā (AS). The previous world ended with Dadi Jaan opening a new blue folder bearing the name YAḤYĀ. This world explores what the Qur’an actually tells us about Yaḥyā: his divinely announced name, his status among the righteous Prophets, the command to hold firmly to Scripture, wisdom granted in youth, compassion, purity, taqwā, dutifulness to parents, absence of arrogance and the peace described for him at three profound stages of existence.

Our principal authorities are Qur’an 3:39, 19:7 and 19:12–15, 21:89–90 and 6:85, explained cautiously with classical Tafsīr. These passages give extraordinary virtues but not a detailed scene-by-scene biography. We therefore do not invent Yaḥyā’s childhood adventures, profession, speeches, death circumstances or journeys. The complete modern narrative belongs to Imaan, Akhlaq, Salaam, Salamah, Dadi Jaan, Sheikh Uncle, Sir Zameer, Mohsin and Mohsina; those fictional situations are applications only and never sacred history.

stories.title: The Name in the Blue Folder
stories.subtitle: A gift from Allah, not a reason to boast

blocks.text: The blue folder had been sitting beside the family’s Qur’an stand since the last exhibition. Across its cover was written a single name: YAḤYĀ. Akhlaq had tried opening it twice, but Dadi Jaan had told him to wait until Imaan returned from her reading group.

Now the two children sat together. Dadi opened the folder and showed them a small card: WHAT CAN A NAME TEACH US? Akhlaq immediately suggested finding out how famous Prophet Yaḥyā had become. Imaan remembered that the Qur’an had already told them something more important: Yaḥyā was the son given to Prophet Zakariyyā after sincere supplication.

Dadi read the meaning of Maryam 19:7. Allah had announced the boy’s name as Yaḥyā. She then explained that Āl ʿImrān 3:39 describes him as a prophet among the righteous. This was a special divine honour, not a name that the children could collect like a badge. The Qur’an gives no reason for them to invent a private childhood conversation or make up the scene of his birth.

At school the next morning, Team Amanah was organising a new exhibit. Mohsin placed his name in enormous letters at the top of the poster because he had brought the paper. Mohsina looked at the list of tasks: Imaan had researched the verses, Akhlaq had sorted the cards, and Sir Zameer had arranged the room. Mohsin was not the whole project.
“I thought my name would help people notice our work,” he said, suddenly embarrassed. Imaan replied, “They can notice everyone’s contribution without anyone becoming more important than the lesson.”

They redesigned the poster. Instead of a giant signature, the heading read: A NAME IS REMEMBERED; GOODNESS IS PRACTISED. Everybody’s contribution appeared in modest print beneath it. When Sheikh Uncle saw the display, he praised the children for distinguishing the honour Allah gave a Prophet from the ordinary effort of a school team.

At home, Akhlaq placed the first card in the new folder. “I don't need the biggest name,” he said. “I need to do something worth doing.” Imaan added a smaller note: Learn the real account first. The blue folder was no longer merely a mystery; it had become a responsibility.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Honour Allah’s special gifts while practising modest, useful effort.

stories.title: The Page That Would Not Stay Open
stories.subtitle: Hold firmly to learning

blocks.text: Rain tapped against the windows at Sheikh Uncle’s Academy. A ceiling fan pushed the children’s notes across their table, and every time Akhlaq turned to the verse he was studying, the page fluttered shut. After three attempts, he pushed his book aside. “It does not want me to learn,” he declared.

Sir Zameer moved the book away from the fan. “The page is not making a decision,” he said. “We are.” He asked the group to consider what it meant to learn with determination. Dadi had already told them about Maryam 19:12: Allah instructed Yaḥyā to take hold of the Scripture with strength and granted him wisdom while still young.

Sheikh Uncle joined them and explained that Ibn Kathīr understood this command as taking the revealed Book seriously—with attention, study and obedience. The special knowledge and wisdom of Yaḥyā were gifts from Allah. The children were not pretending to become him; their smaller lesson was to approach their own Qur’an learning sincerely.

Mohsin proposed a race to see who could read the most pages in five minutes. Mohsina worried that the youngest pupils would lose, especially those who needed more time to read. Imaan suggested three stations instead: read a short passage accurately; ask one real question; identify one good action connected to its meaning. Every learner could work at a suitable pace.

Akhlaq still wanted to finish first. He hurried through his page, then discovered he could not explain the word his teacher asked about. A younger child who had read only two lines could explain both lines with care. Akhlaq returned to his seat and tried again. This time he listened, checked the meaning and asked Sir Zameer for help rather than hiding his confusion.

When the rain stopped, the team had not broken any speed record. But the notes were accurate, and every learner had made progress. Akhlaq drew a little bookmark for the folder: START AGAIN WITH CARE. The page that kept closing had taught him something about reopening his attention.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Study with attention, accuracy, understanding and perseverance.

The academy’s annual question box was overflowing. Children had dropped folded notes inside throughout the week: Why do we pray? How do I know a rumour is true? Can I ask for help when I do not understand? One card simply read, I AM THE YOUNGEST IN THE GROUP. DOES MY QUESTION COUNT?

Akhlaq assumed that the most difficult question should be answered first. Imaan disagreed. “A question matters because someone needs to understand,” she said. “It isn't a competition.” Mohsina suggested they organise the cards by topic and invite every writer to hear the answers without naming them publicly.

Dadi Jaan came for the lesson and read Maryam 19:12 again. Allah had granted Yaḥyā wisdom as a child. She explained that this was a special gift which did not mean every child automatically knows everything. Rather, it reminds adults not to despise the capacity of younger learners—and reminds children to seek knowledge patiently. The Qur’an does not tell us the exact classroom, games or daily routine of Yaḥyā, and none would be invented.

Sir Zameer asked a simple question: “If someone gives an answer confidently, must it be correct?” Mohsin said yes, then hesitated. He remembered a time he had announced the wrong timetable. The teacher showed how to check an answer against reliable evidence rather than a loud voice. Some questions needed an adult expert, not a guess from classmates.

The youngest pupil was invited to ask the first question anonymously. The teachers answered it with care. Nobody laughed. A few older students discovered they had wondered the same thing. Afterward, Akhlaq offered to help organise a second box specifically for questions that were hard to ask aloud.

At home he told Salamah, “Wisdom is not acting as though you know everything.” She smiled. “It also includes admitting what you don't know.” He wrote their new rule on the folder: SMALL VOICES DESERVE A THOUGHTFUL ANSWER.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Honour honest questions and admit what you do not know.

A new reading corner opened at the academy beside a wide window. The sunlight made it cheerful, but one chair stood far from the shelves. When a younger pupil with a walking aid entered, she could not reach the books without asking another child to move the furniture.

Mohsin hurried to carry the chair. “I can fix everything,” he announced. But the pupil asked him to stop. “Please ask me first,” she said. She needed a clear path, not an audience watching her be carried from place to place. Mohsin stepped back, apologised and listened.

During Qur’an time, Sheikh Uncle explained Maryam 19:13. Allah describes Yaḥyā with ḥanān—tenderness or compassion—and purity, and says that he was mindful of Allah. Classical commentators explain this as a special mercy and virtue granted to him. The children could not measure that Prophetic quality in points, but they could consider whether their own manners made another person feel respected.

Sir Zameer asked the team to redesign the corner with its users. Imaan measured the pathway. Mohsina asked which books should be placed on lower shelves. Akhlaq made larger labels so the titles were easier to find. Mohsin carried a shelf only after the group had agreed where it should go. The work took longer than a heroic-looking rescue, yet it served more readers.

At lunch, a child asked why their new display had no “Kindest Person” trophy. Imaan explained that kindness is not always visible; some help is private, and some people need support themselves. A trophy could pressure children to perform generosity rather than practise it. Their class instead kept a list of access improvements for teachers to review.

When the younger pupil returned, she reached her chosen book without anyone rushing to tell her what she needed. “This works better,” she said. Akhlaq quietly placed the fourth card into the blue folder: COMPASSION LISTENS BEFORE IT ACTS. The chair stayed beside the window, but now it was in the right place.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Compassion begins by listening to the person being helped.

stories.title: The Pencil Mark on the Page
stories.subtitle: Purity, mistakes and honest repair

blocks.text: A blue pencil line ran straight across Imaan’s carefully prepared poster. Nobody seemed to know how it got there. The exhibit was due that afternoon, and Mohsin had already begun to guess who must have made the mark.

Akhlaq admitted that he had borrowed the pencil but insisted that he had not touched the poster. Imaan looked at the line, then at the crowded table. “We need to understand what happened before blaming anyone,” she said. Sir Zameer helped them check the materials. The loose pencil had rolled under a heavy folder when the table moved, leaving the mark by accident.

The class lesson that morning concerned the same verse about Yaḥyā: Maryam 19:13 praises purity and taqwā. Dadi had explained that these words describe Allah’s favour and Yaḥyā’s character. They do not justify shaming a child for an accident or pretending that a person with good character never needs to correct a mistake.

Mohsin looked uncomfortable. He had been ready to blame Akhlaq without evidence. “What should I do now?” he asked. Sir Zameer answered, “Begin with the truth. Apologise for an unfair accusation, then help repair what can be repaired.” Mohsin apologised. Akhlaq offered to redraw the affected border, and Imaan accepted the help.

A younger learner noticed that her own worksheet had several mistakes and asked whether it meant she was a bad person. Salamah, who was visiting the class, reminded everyone that a worksheet is not a measure of a heart. People learn, ask forgiveness where needed, and try to improve. The app would never show children a spiritual cleanliness score or rank their private religious feelings.

By afternoon the poster looked different from the first plan, but it was readable. Mohsin wrote “CHECK BEFORE ACCUSING” on a separate practice card, and Akhlaq added “MAKE REPAIRS WITHOUT HIDING THE TRUTH.” Imaan slipped both into the folder. The pencil mark had disappeared, but the responsibility they learned remained.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Truthfulness includes repairing mistakes without humiliation.

stories.title: The Bag at the Front Door
stories.subtitle: Dutifulness with dignity and care

blocks.text: Salaam returned home carrying a small shopping bag and a much heavier box of supplies for the family’s weekend reading activity. Akhlaq rushed forward to prove how strong he had become. He reached for the heavy box, lost his grip for a moment, and set it back down.

“Use your judgment first,” Salaam said kindly. He placed the box on a stable surface and asked Akhlaq to carry the lighter bag instead. Imaan cleared the hallway and Salamah helped organise the supplies. The family had done the task safely together rather than forcing one child to act older than he was.

That evening, Dadi read Maryam 19:14, which describes Yaḥyā as dutiful to his parents, not domineering or disobedient. She explained that obedience to Allah and respectful treatment of parents belong together, and the verse honours a particular Prophet. Children can practise care through speech, listening and appropriate help without being held responsible for adults’ emotional needs or unsafe tasks.

At school, Akhlaq saw two pupils disagreeing over what “helping parents” meant. One thought that only expensive gifts counted. Another argued that a child should obey every instruction, even if frightening or harmful. Sir Zameer corrected both ideas. Good manners can be shown in small ordinary actions, and a child must seek a trustworthy adult when an instruction is unsafe, abusive or asks them to conceal harm.

For their practice task, the children prepared a voluntary family-help menu: put away your own books, speak politely, carry a light item, ask what is needed, and thank a caregiver. The menu also said, “Choose work appropriate for your age and ability; ask for help.” No child would have to submit evidence about home life.

When Akhlaq delivered his light bag to the kitchen, Salaam thanked him. “You helped wisely,” he said. Akhlaq looked at the heavy box, which his father had moved with adult help, and felt no need to compete with it. In the blue folder he wrote: KINDNESS TO FAMILY NEEDS BOTH LOVE AND GOOD SENSE.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Family care should be kind, respectful and safe.

stories.title: Who Gets to Hold the Microphone?
stories.subtitle: Strength without arrogance

blocks.text: The rehearsal for the academy gathering began badly. Mohsin had been appointed group presenter, but he spoke over Imaan, interrupted Mohsina, and announced decisions without asking the other pupils. He was not trying to hurt anyone. He simply believed that a leader should sound important.

When the microphone was passed to Akhlaq, he copied the same loud manner. Within minutes, nobody could hear the actual presentation. Sir Zameer switched the microphone off and invited the team to sit in a circle. “What is leadership supposed to protect?” he asked. The pupils answered slowly: the work, the truth, everyone's chance to contribute, and the needs of listeners.

Sheikh Uncle connected their discussion to Maryam 19:14. The Qur’an tells us that Yaḥyā was not jabbār—overbearing or domineering—and was not disobedient. This was not evidence of a particular meeting or speech in his historical life. It was an authentic description from revelation. Their school scene was only a smaller opportunity to avoid arrogance.

Mohsina suggested a new speaking plan. Imaan would explain the Qur’anic source. Mohsin would describe the modern school example. Akhlaq would introduce the practice activity. A teacher would check the Arabic and meaning before any student read from the approved material. This time Mohsin waited until Imaan finished and thanked her for correcting a reference.

During the second rehearsal the microphone stopped working. The team did not panic. They gathered their listeners closer and spoke slowly. The presentation succeeded without anyone claiming complete credit. When their teacher praised the cooperation, Mohsin said, “I thought leading meant being heard most. It actually meant helping everyone be heard.”

The children put another card into the folder: AUTHORITY MUST NOT BECOME ARROGANCE. Imaan placed it below the verse reference so no one would mistake the fictional microphone incident for part of Prophetic history. Their display had finally learned to speak with a quieter voice.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Leadership protects dignity instead of dominating others.

stories.title: The Page for Tomorrow
stories.subtitle: Peace, the Hereafter and continuing good deeds

blocks.text: The final day of the learning exhibition arrived. Eight stations stood around the hall, each holding a Qur’anic verse, a brief approved explanation and a clearly labelled modern story. At the centre stood the blue folder from Volume Twenty-Two. It was now filled with reminders about listening, study, compassion, family care and humility.

Dadi Jaan asked the children to choose the verse that should close their world. They selected Maryam 19:15: peace upon Yaḥyā on the day he was born, the day he dies and the day he is raised alive. Sheikh Uncle explained gently that the verse honours Yaḥyā at these important stages. It points toward the reality of resurrection and the Hereafter. The Qur’an does not supply the detailed circumstances of his death here; the children would not turn later dramatic accounts into an animated scene.

Akhlaq wondered whether studying the Hereafter meant they should stop enjoying ordinary activities. Salamah answered that remembering accountability should make people more sincere, truthful and caring in daily life. The children were free to learn, play and grow; faith should guide those activities rather than turn every feeling into a spiritual test.

Visitors walked through the exhibition. A younger child chose to listen patiently when her brother was speaking. A father wrote that he wanted to make regular time for family Qur’an study. Mohsina offered to help a new pupil find the correct room. None of the visitors was asked to announce personal sins or prove good deeds to the class.

Before closing, Sir Zameer read al-Anʿām 6:85. The verse names Zakariyyā, Yaḥyā, ʿĪsā and Ilyās among the righteous. Imaan noticed the next name immediately. “ʿĪsā (AS),” she said. Dadi smiled and placed a new card inside the now-closed blue folder. The card read: THE NEXT WORLD BEGINS WITH A MIRACULOUS GIFT.

Akhlaq did not expect the compass to glow. Instead, he checked that every exhibit label still showed the correct Qur’anic reference. “First the truth,” he said, “then the action we carry home.” Dadi agreed. The most meaningful part of the exhibition would be what they practised after the displays were put away.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Remember the Hereafter and carry sincere goodness into daily life.

missions.title: A Name Given in Glad Tidings

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Recognise Yaḥyā as a divinely announced son and Prophet; do not turn a special name into boasting.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Maryam, 19:7: Zakariyyā was given glad tidings of a son named Yaḥyā; the Qur’an describes his name as specially designated.
يَا زَكَرِيَّا إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلَامٍ اسْمُهُ يَحْيَىٰ لَمْ نَجْعَلْ لَهُ مِنْ قَبْلُ سَمِيًّا

discover.label: Working complete āyah
discover.text: Arabic, translation and Tafsīr sign-off required before publication.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: The Qur’an records a special divine announcement to Zakariyyā concerning his son Yaḥyā. This is historical revelation, not an indication that names, family background or popularity determine a child’s worth. The learner should use this source as the boundary of the historical claim and apply its limited character lesson with humility. No modern school or family incident belongs to revelation.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: When do I use a name, title or family connection to feel superior?

missions.question: A class poster has space for several contributors, but one pupil wants only his own name printed.

choices.text: Give fair credit to each contributor while keeping the subject of the lesson central.
choices.feedback: Fair credit protects each helper’s dignity and keeps the lesson central. This is a modern ethical application; it does not represent an incident in Yaḥyā’s historical life.

choices.text: Use the loudest name because popularity makes work more valuable.
choices.feedback: One large name can hide teamwork and make the exhibit about attention. Revisit the verse and try again without penalty.

choices.text: Remove every name and pretend nobody helped.
choices.feedback: Erasing every credit denies the reality of genuine contributions. Revisit the verse and try again without penalty.

missions.action: Thank one person for a real contribution without comparing their value to others.

remember.label: REMEMBER — PRIVATE MUḤĀSABAH
remember.text: When do I use a name, title or family connection to feel superior? Mark “Practised / Still learning / Skip”. Do not publicly rank behaviour or request proof of completion.

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: سَمِيًّا — namesake; نُبَشِّرُكَ — We give you glad tidings

missions.title: Prophethood Is Allah’s Choice

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN

missions.question: A pupil receives a learning certificate and claims it proves that Allah loves them more than others.

choices.text: Congratulate the effort, while explaining that awards cannot measure Allah’s judgement of hearts.
choices.feedback: Celebrate worthwhile study while acknowledging that only Allah knows a person’s standing. This is a modern ethical application; it does not represent an incident in Yaḥyā’s historical life.

choices.text: Agree that the certificate proves superior faith.
choices.feedback: A certificate measures a school task, not divine approval or Prophethood. Revisit the verse and try again without penalty.

choices.text: Say everyone who receives an award is showing off.
choices.feedback: A lawful award can be received gratefully without boasting. Revisit the verse and try again without penalty.

missions.action: Praise one effort without claiming to know someone’s private standing before Allah.

missions.title: Compassion Without an Audience

missions.question: A classmate cannot comfortably reach the new library shelf.

choices.text: Ask what would make access easier, and work with the teacher to improve the room.

choices.text: Ignore the difficulty because it does not affect you.
choices.feedback: A difficulty deserves attention even when it does not inconvenience you. Revisit the verse and try again without penalty.

missions.title: Purity and a Sincere Intention

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN

وَحَنَانًا مِنْ لَدُنَّا وَزَكَاةً ۖ وَكَانَ تَقِيًّا

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Do I improve my conduct or only try to appear good?

missions.question: Someone accidentally marks a group poster and is afraid everyone will call them bad.

choices.text: Hide the incident and blame another pupil.
choices.feedback: Hiding a mistake and blaming another person creates another wrong. Revisit the verse and try again without penalty.

choices.text: Explain what happened honestly, repair the page and avoid shaming anyone.
choices.feedback: Truth, repair and a calm apology are better than denial or shame. This is a modern ethical application; it does not represent an incident in Yaḥyā’s historical life.

choices.text: Announce a public list of children who make mistakes.
choices.feedback: A public mistake list humiliates learners and is not evidence of taqwā. Revisit the verse and try again without penalty.

missions.action: Correct one small mistake truthfully, without humiliating yourself or someone else.

missions.question: At home there are two bags: one light and one too heavy for a child.

missions.question: A child is told by an older person to conceal a frightening or harmful act.

synthesis.text: Allah’s gift is not an ordinary achievement

From the annunciation of his name to his being counted among the righteous Prophets, Yaḥyā’s account begins with divine favour. Āl ʿImrān 3:39 and Maryam 19:7 establish what can be taught as revelation. The child’s takeaway is gratitude and accurate knowledge, never the idea that a certificate, family name or app reward creates Prophetic rank. Giving fair credit and resisting pride are contemporary ethical applications, not claims about a scene from his life.
Learning with firmness, not performance

Maryam 19:12 directs Yaḥyā to hold fast to the Scripture and records wisdom granted to him as a child. Classical Tafsīr highlights understanding, seriousness and commitment. A younger pupil should therefore find questions welcome and careful study meaningful. An app must avoid speed-based Qur’an contests, comparison of religious ability or declarations that one learner is spiritually above another.
Compassion and purity belong together

Maryam 19:13 describes ḥanān, purity and taqwā. These are not merely attractive labels: the verse honours real goodness. Children may practise considerate listening, noticing access needs and being truthful when they make mistakes. They must not be asked to disclose their thoughts, report private sins or prove the condition of their hearts to an algorithm. Genuine kindness protects another person’s dignity.
Respect without domination

Maryam 19:14 joins dutifulness toward parents with freedom from arrogance and disobedience. A child can speak respectfully, help at home safely and consider other people in group projects. Such teaching never cancels a child’s right to seek protection from danger or disclose harm to a trustworthy adult. The negative example of overbearing behaviour is particularly useful in leadership: authority should make room for the quietest voice.
Peace, resurrection and the lasting horizon

Maryam 19:15 describes peace upon Yaḥyā at birth, at death and upon being raised alive. It points to Allah’s honour and the Hereafter, without providing licence to invent tragic scenes. Al-Anʿām 6:85 remembers him among the righteous. The child’s goal is not to imitate a Prophet’s unique standing but to keep Allah in mind and practise consistent goodness with humility.
CARRY FORWARD • Hold firmly to authentic learning. Listen compassionately. Repair mistakes truthfully. Serve family safely. Lead without arrogance. Remember Allah and the Hereafter.
